clips.title: How Grouping Works | Sentry Tutorials
clips.why: Sentry has the same problem we have, thousands of events for one bug, and solves it the same way: it hashes the parts that matter and groups every event with that hash.
look: Some details feed the hash and some are ignored on purpose, like file names and the error's value. That is our normalising step.
Every event that gets the same hash lands in one group, the way every red build with one fingerprint lands in one run.
A missing file and bad JSON stay two separate groups, just like a lint error and a type error in the same check job.
clips.after: Our trigger service does what you just watched Sentry do, with one difference: the hash becomes a Temporal workflow ID, so one group means one fixer.
clips.quote: every event that shares this hash will go into the same group

clips.title: Setting custom fingerprints to reduce noise
clips.why: When the default grouping is not good enough, you pick the fingerprint yourself, which is exactly the choice we make for red builds.
look: The advice is to look for what is unique about the problem and build the fingerprint from that, and nothing else.
A fingerprint can join events into one group or split them apart. Our error line splits, the dropped timestamps and paths join.
Notice that he wants fewer alerts. Fewer, better groups is the same goal as fewer, better fixers.
clips.after: Our fingerprint rule is fixed in code: last green commit, failing job names and each job's normalised first error line, and never the pushed commit.
clips.quote: look at unique characteristics of that issue

clips.title: Temporal Live Coding Demo: Handling Failures & Human Interaction
clips.why: You see a real Temporal signal arrive at a running workflow: a handler flips a value and the waiting workflow carries on.
look: The signal handler does one small job when the message arrives, like our addTrigger handler pushing a red build onto the list.
While the workflow waits, the worker is not busy with it at all. That is why our gather window holds no machine.
The signal reaches a workflow that is already running. signalWithStart adds one thing: it starts the run first if none is open.
clips.after: Swap 'approve order' for 'addTrigger' and the order for a red build, and this is how the 10:05 build reaches the fixer that started at 10:02.
clips.quote: temporal signals which is how you interact with running workflows

clips.title: Idempotency - What it is and How to Implement it
clips.why: An idempotency key is the classic answer to 'do this once, however many times I am asked', and our workflow ID is one: a key, kept for a while, that makes repeats harmless.
look: One way to build the key is to hash the request body. That is our fingerprint, built from the failure instead of a request.
The SpongeBob towel: two identical requests are not always duplicates. For us the last green commit is what tells Tuesday's break from Thursday's.
The keys are kept for a while and then expire. Temporal keeps a closed workflow ID for its thirty days of history, which is why REJECT_DUPLICATE can still say no.
clips.after: The difference is what a repeat gets: a payment API replays the old answer, while our trigger service treats a returning fingerprint as a sign the fix did not hold and calls a person.
clips.quote: Another option is to hash the body of the request.

practice.q: Here is the first error line from a red build: "2026-10-14T10:01:22.2113356Z FAIL src/projects/ProjectsTable.test.tsx > shows the owner (48ms) in /tmp/ci-8sK2pq". Which part do you KEEP for the fingerprint?

options.why: Strip it. The timestamp is new on every run, so keeping it would give every red build its own fixer.
Keep it. This is what broke: the file and the test name stay exactly the same on every build until main is fixed.
Strip it. The same failing test runs a little faster or slower each time, so the duration says nothing about the problem.
Strip it, or replace it with /tmp/x. The temporary folder gets a new random name on every run.

practice.q: In the idempotency clip, two orders for the same SpongeBob towel look identical but are not duplicates. In our fingerprint, which part tells Tuesday's broken test apart from the same test breaking again on Thursday, after main was green in between?

options.why: Main went green, so the last green commit moved. Same job, same error line, but a new fingerprint, so Thursday gets a fresh fixer.
The same test fails in the same job both days, so the job names are identical and cannot tell the two breaks apart.
It would tell them apart, but it would also tell every red build apart, giving each one its own fixer. That is why we leave it out.

practice.q: Name the Temporal call that either tells the open run or starts it.
practice.before: If a run with this workflow ID is open,
practice.after: sends it the addTrigger signal; if none is open, it starts the run and then delivers the signal.
practice.hint: Two actions in one name: send a message, or begin.
practice.why: signalWithStart does both in one operation, so two red builds arriving at the same moment still cannot start two runs.

practice.q: Fill in the reuse policy that stops a closed fingerprint from starting a second fixer.
practice.hint: By default a closed run frees its name. This policy refuses instead.
practice.why: With REJECT_DUPLICATE, an ID whose run has closed may not start again, so a returning root cause comes back as an error and goes to a person.

practice.q: Main breaks at 10:02 and more red builds follow. Put the steps in order, from the first red build to one fixer at work.
items: A build on main goes red and is reported to the trigger service
The trigger service normalises each failing job's first error line and hashes it with the last green commit and the job names
signalWithStart on cifix:fcp:<fingerprint> starts the CI fixer run, with the build as its first trigger
The run sleeps through the seven-minute gather window while later red builds arrive as addTrigger signals
The window ends and the run checks that main is still red and passes its safety gates
The run claims a VM and the fixer starts with every red build in hand
practice.why: The name comes first, because it decides which run a build joins. The waiting comes before the VM, so the fixer plans with all the evidence and no machine sits idle.

practice.q: The fixer's run closed at 11:00, but its fix never landed and main stayed red. At 11:20 a red build arrives with exactly the same fingerprint. What happens?

options.text: A new fixer run starts and tries again
options.why: Not with REJECT_DUPLICATE. The closed ID may not start again, and a second try would most likely repeat the first one.

options.text: The build is added to the closed run as a signal
options.why: Only an open run can receive a signal. With no open run, signalWithStart tries to start one, and Temporal refuses.

options.text: Temporal refuses the start and the trigger service posts the problem to #ai-agents-alerts
options.why: The same fingerprint after its run closed means main has not been green since. The trigger service expects the 'already started' error, does not retry, and hands it to a person.
